title: Bernoulli Distribution
body:
One trial, two outcomes, success with probability $p$ and failure with $1-p$. $X$ takes the value
$1$ or $0$, which makes it an **indicator variable**: it is $1$ exactly when the event happened.

$$
E[X] = p, \qquad \text{Var}(X) = p(1-p)
$$

Both fall straight out of the definitions, and the variance is largest at $p = 0.5$ and zero at
$p = 0$ or $1$, which is the sensible answer: a certain outcome has no spread.

It is the atom the rest of block 2 is built from. $n$ independent Bernoulli trials summed give a
**binomial**, the number of trials until the first success gives a **geometric**, and a great many
awkward expectations become easy by writing the variable as a sum of indicators and using linearity
of expectation. See [[Probability Distribution]] and [[Random Variable]].

A proportion is a Bernoulli mean, which is why $\hat{p}$ has standard error $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ and
why every confidence interval and test for a proportion in blocks 3 and 4 is really a statement
about this distribution. It is also the model behind a [[Binary Classification|binary label]], so
[[Logistic Regression]] is the fitting of a Bernoulli whose $p$ depends on the input.
